claims.text: The Trump administration proposed a new $103,265 fee for cap-subject H-1B petitions.
A previous $100,000 H-1B payment introduced under a September 2025 presidential proclamation is set to expire in September 2026 unless extended.
The US Department of Homeland Security proposed the new $103,265 fee as an additional charge on top of existing H-1B filing and statutory fees.
Higher education institutions, affiliated non-profits, and research organizations are eligible to hire cap-exempt H-1B workers without paying cap-subject fees.
The annual statutory cap for new H-1B visas is 85,000, which includes 65,000 regular visas and 20,000 visas reserved under the Master's cap.

Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, stated that the proposed $103,265 fee is tied to whether an H-1B petition is cap-subject rather than whether the worker is physically inside or outside the US.
New York-based immigration attorney Cyrus D Mehta called the proposed $103,265 fee preposterous and stated that the Trump administration has killed the goose that laid the golden eggs.
Indian nationals received 283,000 H-1B visas, including extensions, in the fiscal year ended 2025, representing 70% of the total allotted.
Indian nationals received nearly 58,000 new H-1B visas for initial employment in the fiscal year ended 2025.
The US Department of Homeland Security estimates the proposed $103,265 fee would generate approximately $8.78 billion annually based on 85,000 cap-subject petitions.
The US Department of Homeland Security estimates 14,541 small entities would be affected by the proposed fee, with 76% facing cost increases exceeding 1% of annual revenue.
The US Department of Homeland Security published the proposed $103,265 H-1B visa fee rule in the Federal Register on Monday, opening a 30-day public comment period.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services received only 85 payments of the $100,000 fee from 70 employers as of February 15.
H-1B visa application government fees typically ranged from $2,000 to $5,000 prior to recent fee increases.
Employers registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas last year, representing a decline of over 25 percent from 2024 and down from 794,000 in 2023.
In August, the US Department of Homeland Security introduced additional fees of up to $4,500 for applications to extend H-1B stays or transfer overseas employees to the US.
The H-1B program allows US employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations for an initial period of up to three years, extendable up to six years.
The US Department of Homeland Security could finalize the proposed H-1B fee regulation by the end of 2026.
On June 8, 2026, the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated agency guidance implementing the $100,000 H-1B fee requirement in State of California v. Mullin.
On July 24, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit rejected the Trump administration's request to stay the District Court ruling against the $100,000 fee.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services has already received enough petitions to reach the 65,000 regular cap and 20,000 master's cap for fiscal year 2027.
According to Boundless Immigration CEO Xiao Wang, top H-1B sponsors in fiscal year 2025 shifted to companies including Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Google.
Boundless Immigration client data showed senior Level III candidates achieved a 68% selection rate in the March 2026 H-1B cap season compared to 40% for entry-level Level I candidates.
The proposed End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026 proposes a three-year pause on new H-1B visas, a reduction of the annual cap to 25,000, and a minimum annual salary threshold of $200,000.
